purpose: Fluticasone furoate is used to help control and prevent symptoms like a stuffy or runny nose, sneezing, and itchy eyes caused by allergies. It is also used in some inhalers to help people with asthma or COPD breathe more easily. It works best when used regularly, not just when symptoms flare up.
how_it_works: This medication is a type of steroid that calms down inflammation and irritation in your nose or airways. Think of it like putting out a fire — it reduces the swelling and redness that causes your symptoms. Because it works locally where you use it (nose or lungs), very little gets into the rest of your body, making it generally very safe for long-term use.
common_side_effects: For the nasal spray: headache, nosebleeds, sore throat, or a runny nose. For the inhaler: throat irritation, hoarseness, or a cough. Some people may get a mild fungal infection (thrush) in the mouth when using an inhaler — rinsing your mouth with water after each use helps prevent this.
warnings: Do not stop using this medication suddenly without talking to your doctor, especially if you have been using it for a long time. It does not work right away for breathing emergencies — always have a rescue inhaler on hand for sudden asthma attacks. Tell your doctor if you have had recent eye problems like cataracts or glaucoma, as long-term steroid use can sometimes affect the eyes. Also let your doctor know if you have any infections, since steroids can make it harder for your body to fight them.
typical_dosing: Nasal spray (Veramyst): Usually 2 sprays in each nostril once a day to start. Once symptoms improve, your doctor may lower it to 1 spray per nostril daily. Inhaler (Arnuity Ellipta): Typically one puff (inhalation) once a day at the same time each day. Always follow the specific instructions your doctor gives you, since the dose can vary based on your condition.
